source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL
finding: Eigenoptions (options from proto-value-function eigenvectors) improve exploration. Options that only go to bottleneck doorways do not. The first eigenoptions found are not the bottlenecks.
numbers: Diffusion time (expected random-walk steps between two random states) in rooms domains. With options added in eigenvalue order, diffusion time first got worse, then fell well below the primitive-action random walk once enough options were present. In the 4-room domain, bottleneck-only options raised diffusion time.
quote: options traditionally used in the literature to speed up planning hinder the agents' performance if used for random exploration
limits: Tabular and linear-feature settings; Atari results are qualitative only. Few options can hurt exploration because long options bias the walk.
agent_relevance: A subgoal library built only from bottlenecks can hurt open-ended search. Use options at several scales and enough of them.

source: Machado et al. (2017) appendix: random-option control
finding: Sequences of randomly chosen subgoal options mostly fail to cut diffusion time, so eigenoptions do more than reach arbitrary states.
numbers: Random option sets raised diffusion time by several orders of magnitude (log axis) until hundreds of options made the graph almost fully connected. In the learning task no single random-option run matched eigenoptions; in some runs the goal was never reached.
limits: Tabular 4-room-type domains; exact run counts per curve not read.
agent_relevance: Which subgoals you pick matters. A random subgoal list is worse than none until it is huge.

source: Machado, Rosenbaum, Guo, Liu, Tesauro, Campbell (2018) Eigenoption discovery through the deep successor representation
finding: Eigenpurposes can be taken from a learned successor representation (SR) instead of the graph Laplacian. It works from samples and from pixels. In 3 of 4 Atari games the options reach corners and useful places; in Freeway it was ineffective.
numbers: SR learned from only 100 episodes in the rooms domain already cut diffusion time considerably. Atari: 500,000 samples per game, 10 passes, RMSProp step 1e-4, then 50,000 random-policy steps. Bank Heist, Montezuma's Revenge, Ms. Pac-Man worked; Freeway did not.
limits: Atari evidence is qualitative (visitation plots). Options were approximated by a greedy one-step emulator lookahead. Authors say this myopia likely missed the key in Montezuma and caused the Freeway failure.
agent_relevance: SR gives subgoals from experience without a graph. Failure case: where short-term greedy control cannot reach the subgoal.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2023) Temporal Abstraction in RL with the Successor Representation (JMLR 24)
finding: Review plus new simulations. Eigenoptions speed up Q-learning with as few as four options. Covering options did not, and were brittle when the SR was learned online.
numbers: Ten sampled gridworld tasks, 50 runs, 99% CI: four eigenoptions never hurt in any task; covering options gave no gain in all ten. With the SR learned online, covering options raised average diffusion time substantially. The option keyboard cut the number of eigenoptions needed by 30% (open room, needs 10) and 42% (four-room, needs 12).
limits: Tabular and small domains. The reason given for covering-option failure (sparse initiation set, one eigenvector) is a conjecture.
agent_relevance: Prefer sets of subgoals that span many directions over single-cut subgoals. Combining options cheaply keeps the library small.

source: Gomez, Bowling, Machado (2024) Proper Laplacian Representation Learning (ALLO), ICLR
finding: Earlier deep Laplacian methods (GDO, GGDO) have a rotation problem and need hyperparameters tuned using the true answer. ALLO fixes this and gives ordered eigenvectors and eigenvalues.
numbers: Best barrier coefficient for GGDO differs by environment (cosine similarity to the true eigenvectors, 60 seeds, 95% CI). ALLO recovers close approximations of the smallest eigenvectors in all three grid environments.
limits: Grid worlds with a known Laplacian; scaling to rich domains not shown in what was read.
agent_relevance: One reason eigen-subgoal results from 2017-2019 were hard to reproduce: the learner was ill-posed and tuned on the answer.

source: Wu, Tucker, Nachum (2019) The Laplacian in RL: learning representations with efficient approximations
finding: Gives the graph-drawing objective (GDO) to learn Laplacian eigenfunctions from sampled transitions in deep RL.
numbers: Only the abstract and method text were read; no results figures recorded.
limits: Any rotation of the eigenvectors also minimises this objective (shown later by Gomez 2024).
agent_relevance: Predecessor of the deep Laplacian options line.

source: Klissarov & Machado (2023) Deep Laplacian-based Options for Temporally-Extended Exploration (DCEO)
finding: Deep covering eigenoptions work in pixel tasks. They match or beat count-based, RND, z-greedy and DIAYN. In Montezuma's Revenge the first eigenfunctions already point to stepping stones toward the key.
numbers: Largest margin over baselines in the Maze task and in Obstructed Key (but the count baseline had perfect counts). DIAYN did not improve on DDQN in the Nine-rooms task. Montezuma and MiniWorld evidence is qualitative eigenfunction plots.
limits: Episodes at most 100 steps. Rubik's cube used a tabular actor because DDQN could not learn. Montezuma result is a plot, not a score.
agent_relevance: Eigenfunction subgoals can be found with few eigenfunctions if the learner is sound.

source: Jinnai, Abel, Hershkowitz, Littman, Konidaris (2019) Finding Options that Minimize Planning Time
finding: Choosing the best set of options for planning is NP-hard, even for deterministic MDPs. So every option-discovery rule is a heuristic with known worst cases.
numbers: Hard to approximate within 2^(log^(1-e) n) unless NP is in DTIME(n^polylog n); (log n)-hard in deterministic MDPs unless P=NP; algorithm A-MOMI gives an O(log n) approximation for deterministic MDPs. Heuristics (betweenness, eigenoptions) were compared in grid domains.
limits: Theory. The optimal sets cost more to compute than solving the MDP, so they only serve to judge heuristics.
agent_relevance: No free lunch: any subgoal-selection rule our agent uses will fail on some structure.

source: Jinnai, Park, Abel, Konidaris (2019) Discovering Options for Exploration by Minimizing Cover Time
finding: Covering options add an edge between the Fiedler-vector extremes to cut expected cover time. They differ from eigenoptions: the k-th covering option minimises algebraic connectivity of the graph augmented with the earlier ones.
numbers: Reported to speed learning in six discrete sparse-reward domains where the true graph is given and the reward must be found.
limits: Needs the transition graph. Machado 2023 found no gain from covering options in ten other tasks, so rival results exist.
agent_relevance: A discriminating case between rival subgoal rules: the ranking depends on setup.

source: Nachum, Tang, Lu, Gu, Lee, Levine (2019) Why does hierarchy (sometimes) work so well in RL?
finding: Most of the benefit of HRL comes from better exploration, not from easier policy learning or imposed structure. A flat agent trained on the hierarchical agent's data is nearly as good.
numbers: Ant tasks (AntMaze, AntPush, AntBlock, AntBlockMaze), 5 seeds, 10M steps. Training horizon only mattered in that c_train > 1. A non-hierarchical shadow agent with multi-step rewards matched HRL on all tasks except AntMaze (slight drop). Hierarchy-inspired exploration methods were competitive with HRL.
quote: most of the observed benefits of hierarchy can be attributed to improved exploration
limits: Fixed-length options only, fully observed Markov tasks, ant locomotion. Authors say conclusions are empirical and limited to these tasks.
agent_relevance: If the gain from subgoals is mostly diversity of exploration, test the subgoal scaffold against a plain multi-attempt baseline.

source: Jong, Hester, Stone (2008) The utility of temporal abstraction in RL, as summarised by Nachum et al. (2019)
finding: Earlier study (reported secondhand): option benefits came mainly from exploration, and only with specially designed options plus prior task knowledge. Most of the rest came from experience replay; replay alone matched it.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary text. Original not opened.
limits: Secondhand; gridworld tasks.
agent_relevance: Long-standing doubt: the hierarchy effect has been confounded with replay and exploration since 2008.

source: Solway, Diuk, Cordova, Yee, Barto, Niv, Botvinick (2014) Optimal behavioral hierarchy, PLoS Comput Biol
finding: The optimal hierarchy minimises expected trial-and-error search, and its borders fall at graph bottlenecks. Four experiments show people choose bottleneck nodes as subgoals.
numbers: Exp 1 N=40: bottleneck bus stops chosen first 4.4 times as often as other locations. Exp 2 N=10 and Exp 3 N=21 (19-node graph): bottleneck chosen first, and recognised faster than an adjacent node (98% accuracy). Exp 4 N=35 Tower of Hanoi: 17 used the single-boundary route most, 7 the reverse, 11 neither.
limits: Students aged 18-21. Deterministic reversible graphs, two-level hierarchies, optimal policies given. Genetic-algorithm search, no guaranteed optimum. Authors do not claim people compute model evidence.
agent_relevance: Supports a bottleneck-based subgoal library, but only shown on small known graphs.

source: Tomov, Yagati, Kumar, Yang, Gershman (2020) Discovery of hierarchical representations for efficient planning, PLoS Comput Biol
finding: A Bayesian model that infers a two-level graph partition by MCMC reproduces the older bottleneck and community-structure results and predicts new planning biases in new experiments.
numbers: Simulation of Solway data (N=40): 65% of choices on bottleneck nodes. Exp 1 N=87: 58/87 made the hierarchy-predicted move, p=0.003. Exp 2 N=241: bad-structure group 53/78 made the biased move; bad vs control chi2=6.52, p=0.01; control vs good no difference (p=0.5). Exp 3 N=127: boundary transitions slower, F=121. Exp 4 N=77: 51/77 showed the bias, p=0.0014.
limits: Parameters hand-picked, not fit. MTurk samples. Exp 3 effect smaller than predicted. Control condition near chance in Exp 2, so graph learning is open. Text after Exp 4 not read.
agent_relevance: Hierarchy causes planning errors: people prefer a path with fewer boundaries even when it is worse. The agent's decomposition can mislead the same way.

source: Ribas-Fernandes, Solway, Diuk, McGuire, Barto, Niv, Botvinick (2011) A neural signature of hierarchical RL, Neuron
finding: Brain activity tracks pseudo-reward prediction errors (change in distance to a subgoal) separately from change in distance to the final goal. Dorsal anterior cingulate is the main site.
numbers: EEG N=9: negativity at Cz (p<0.01). fMRI Exp 1, 30 analysed: dorsal ACC tracks PPE size, peak Talairach (0,9,39), cluster-corrected p<0.01, kept after controlling for subgoal displacement. Exp 2, 14 analysed: right accumbens positive PPE, p<0.05. Behaviour N=22: goal distance predicted package choice (-7.6, p<0.001); subgoal distance did not (p=0.43). Mean Bayes factor 4.31 for HRL over a model rewarding subgoal attainment.
limits: Small samples. Reverse inference, partial control for response conflict. Accumbens negative-PPE result null. ACC role in feedback negativity disputed.
agent_relevance: Subgoals act as their own reward stream. The agent can score subgoal progress separately from goal progress.

source: Momennejad, Russek, Cheong, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman (2017) The successor representation in human RL, Nat Hum Behav
finding: Human revaluation is not pure model-free, pure model-based or pure SR. A hybrid SR plus model-based mix fit best. Reward revaluation was easier than transition revaluation.
numbers: Exp 1 n=58: revaluation score reward .52, transition .45, control .03; reward vs transition t(57)=2.89, p<0.01. Exp 2 (MTurk, n=88 of 112): switch rate reward .66, transition .47, policy .50, control .08; reward vs transition Z=-2.85, p=.0034.
limits: Pure SR failed because transition revaluation was above control. No log-likelihoods in the text; 24 of 112 excluded in Exp 2; one test trial per block; the hybrid is called a rough proxy.
agent_relevance: SR-derived subgoals rest on a representation people use only partly, and one that updates slowly when transitions change.

source: Eckstein & Collins (2020) Computational evidence for hierarchically structured RL in humans, PNAS
finding: Only a hierarchical RL model (task sets plus actions) reproduced all human patterns. Flat RL could not produce task-set perseveration or reactivation.
numbers: Main N=26 analysed. Switch cost context > stimulus t(25)=3.47, p=0.002. Comparison-phase preference Bayes factor 1171.65 for hierarchical vs flat RL; accuracy BF 39.64; hidden-context reactivation BF 5.12. Several BFs weak (1.49 to 1.78). Three samples; the majority of results replicated, the RT effect only in the replication.
limits: Hierarchy here is choice abstraction (task sets), not temporal abstraction over subgoals. Several effects at p about 0.045 to 0.048. Reporting inconsistencies noted (trial counts, a z/p pair). Students only.
agent_relevance: Evidence for task-set reuse, not for subgoal discovery.

source: Xia & Collins (2021) Temporal and state abstractions for efficient learning, transfer and composition in humans, Psych Rev
finding: People learn reusable options and reuse them in new contexts, which causes negative transfer when the old option no longer fits. An option model fits the error pattern best.
numbers: Exp 1 in-lab n=25, MTurk n=55. In lab, Block 8 option-transfer errors exceeded other errors, t(24)=2.5, p=0.02; MTurk replicated this (t(54)=4.7, p<0.0001). The first-stage negative transfer did not replicate on MTurk (F=0.19, p=0.83). Exp 3 (non-Markov structure removed): option-transfer vs other not significant in lab (t(23)=0.8, p=0.43).
limits: Only 55 of 116 and 31 of 65 MTurk participants kept (exclusion by first-stage performance). Hierarchical models compared by simulation, not fit. Several effects marginal (p=0.055, 0.06). Exp 4 not read.
agent_relevance: Learned options transfer, and also interfere. Test the subgoal library for negative transfer when a task looks the same but is not.

source: Li & Collins (2025) Algorithmic account of how humans learn, transfer and compose hierarchically structured decision policies, Cognition
finding: A large sample replicates negative transfer of learned options and finds a meta-learning model fits better than a fully hierarchical model.
numbers: N=1,026, over 1 million choices. Clusters: 181 random, 254 mid, 591 best performers. Negative transfer in Block 7 replicated Xia & Collins. Meta model beat hierarchical model by AIC, t=24, p<1e-4. V1 vs V2 transfer did not differ (t=0.28, p=0.78). A backward-in-time representation fit better than a forward one in every V3 condition (for example V3-V3 t=-7.1).
limits: Main findings hold for about 75% of participants. Students from one institution. Stage-1 policies not modelled. V3 advantage weak, significant only in some subsamples.
agent_relevance: Rival to explicit options: a learned compressed policy prior may explain behaviour without subgoals.

source: Czechowski et al. (2021, v4 2026) Subgoal Search for Complex Reasoning Tasks (kSubS)
finding: A transformer proposes subgoals k steps ahead inside best-first search. It beats low-level search on Rubik's Cube, Sokoban and the INT inequality prover.
numbers: Rubik's Cube: BF-kSubS solves nearly 100% of cubes, plain BestFS under 10%. Sokoban: with graph size 1000 it beats the expert that made the data (expert success 78%, 67%, 60% on three board sizes), up to 20x20 boards. INT: the older network got 92% at L=5; their transformer baseline already solved over 99%. Of generated subgoals, 17% increase the distance to solution and 5% reach dead states.
limits: Small trained transformer, not a general LLM. Subgoal quality imperfect, fixed k.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a subgoal generator inside search, and a warning that a sizeable share of proposed subgoals are bad, so verify them.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: Decomposing only when the executor LLM fails beats iterative acting, plan-and-execute and retry with reflection.
numbers: GPT-3.5 ALFWorld all-task success (dmax=3): ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Try-again 47.8, Reflexion 57.5, ADaPT 71.6. Claimed gains up to 28.3 points (ALFWorld), 27 (WebShop), 33 (TextCraft). Pick2 task: ADaPT 52.9 vs 5.9 to 11.8 for the others. On the Look task ADaPT tied three baselines at 61.1 (ReAct 55.6).
limits: Decomposition is by LLM prompting, not discovered from data. Gains vary by task; some sub-tasks unchanged. Table read for one executor model.
agent_relevance: Recursive as-needed decomposition is a working subgoal policy for LLM agents: split only on failure.

source: Zhao, Li, Kong (2023) Decomposing the Enigma: subgoal-based demonstration learning for formal theorem proving
finding: Subgoals written into the demonstration examples raise LLM proof success on miniF2F. Diffusion-chosen example sets add more.
numbers: miniF2F proof accuracy 38.9% to 44.3% with subgoal-based demonstrations; 45.5% with diffusion-based demonstration organisation; reported 5x sampling-efficiency gain over the previous best method.
limits: Subgoals are written per demonstration and refined, not discovered at test time. Only the abstract-level numbers were read.
agent_relevance: Subgoals in the prompt help; the gain is modest (5.4 points).

source: Jinnai et al. (2019) versus Machado et al. (2023): rival-rule disagreement
finding: Covering options were designed to beat eigenoptions at exploration, yet in Machado's ten-task test they gave no gain.
numbers: Machado 2023: four eigenoptions helped or did not hurt in all ten tasks; covering options helped in none. Jinnai 2019 reports covering gains in six domains.
limits: Different protocols, task sets, and whether the graph or the SR was known.
agent_relevance: The winner among discovery rules depends on setup. Do not hard-code one rule.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2018) Count-based exploration with the successor representation
finding: Related: the SR norm gives a count-like exploration bonus. Removing the bonus from DQN-MMC+SR hurts Montezuma's Revenge a lot.
numbers: The text says the bonus has a big impact in Montezuma's Revenge; exact scores not recorded.
limits: Not an option method; the exploration alternative to options.
agent_relevance: A cheaper alternative to a subgoal library for hard-exploration tasks.

source: Vezhnevets et al. (2017) FeUdal Networks for hierarchical RL
finding: Manager sets goals in latent space for a worker. Cited by the eigenoption papers as hierarchy built on learned latent states.
numbers: Not read for numbers.
limits: PDF downloaded, only the title was checked.
agent_relevance: Related work.

source: Bacon, Harb, Precup (2017) The Option-Critic Architecture
finding: End-to-end learning of options and policy; options baseline in Nachum 2019 (through Frans et al.).
numbers: Not read for numbers.
limits: PDF downloaded, only the title was checked.
agent_relevance: Related work.
